title: Introduction to Server-Side Programming
subtopics: Why logic may be placed in the database

learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Introduction to Server-Side Programming.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to why logic may be placed in the database.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Introduction to Server-Side Programming. Its primary job is to help you move reusable rules into server-side functions, procedures and triggers only when their behavior stays testable. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing introduction to server-side programming teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: move reusable rules into server-side functions, procedures and triggers only when their behavior stays testable. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Introduction to Server-Side Programming
content_blocks.expected_output: Emits a NOTICE from an anonymous PL/pgSQL block when PL/pgSQL is available (normally installed by default).
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a scratch session; DO executes the block once without creating a permanent routine.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Version note: PostgreSQL 18.6 is the primary reference. PostgreSQL 19 beta/development features are not assumed to be stable.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Introduction to Server-Side Programming”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Why logic may be placed in the database”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Why logic may be placed in the database”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Introduction to Server-Side Programming, with an explanation of “Why logic may be placed in the database”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Introduction to Server-Side Programming fits into the broader goal to move reusable rules into server-side functions, procedures and triggers only when their behavior stays testable.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Why logic may be placed in the database, PostgreSQL function and procedure concepts, SQL-language routines.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
